extracted.intended_audience: federal agency analysts and policymakers preparing regulatory impact analyses and benefit-cost analyses
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and standards for preparing regulatory impact analyses (benefit-cost analyses) under OMB Circular A-4, including treatment of valuation methods, non-monetized effects, transfers, compliance, distributional analyses, and related methodological choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice between willingness-to-pay (WTP) and willingness-to-accept (WTA)
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies should recognize WTP and WTA as distinct measures that “simply differ in who starts with the good or service” and that available evidence may constrain choice of WTP vs WTA measures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not adopt a blanket preference for WTP or WTA; use professional judgment to determine the most appropriate available evidence. Agencies may use WTP or WTA as proxies for one another when justified (e.g., when the WTA premium over WTP cannot be explained as rational behavior). Example: many VSL estimates derive from wage compensation (a WTA context).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of revealed-preference and stated-preference methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies should follow a balanced and credible perspective on the appropriate use of revealed and stated preference methods consistent with contemporary economic literature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Updated material supports both methods where appropriate; agencies should consider methodological tradeoffs, quality of evidence, and recent advances in the literature when choosing and applying these methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of benefit-transfer methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Benefit-transfer methods are an accepted analytic approach and the proposed revisions provide updated material on their use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies may use benefit-transfer when direct valuation is unavailable, but should consider the applicability and limitations of transferred estimates to the regulatory context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include additional benefits and costs (direct, indirect, intended, unintended)
rubrics_metrics.description: Benefit-cost analysis (BCA) should include all the significant consequences of a policy decision—whether direct or indirect, intended or unintended, beneficial or harmful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies should list categories of benefits and costs to achieve transparency so readers can judge which effects are consistent with the regulation’s purposes. OMB does not require analysts to determine which regulatory purposes are the 'main' ones or to adjudicate what Congress had in mind.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency via listing categories rather than adjudicating 'main purpose'
rubrics_metrics.description: Instead of instructing analysts to identify a regulation’s 'main purpose,' OMB advises clearly listing categories of benefits and costs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Listing categories allows readers to categorize effects themselves and avoids placing analysts in the improper role of determining which purposes Congress had in mind.

rubrics_metrics.name: Terminology: 'additional benefits and costs' vs 'ancillary benefits and costs'
rubrics_metrics.description: The draft moved from 'ancillary benefits and countervailing risks' to 'additional benefits and costs' to clarify that 'ancillary' or 'indirect' effects are not meaningfully different from 'primary' or 'direct' effects analytically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OMB favored 'additional benefits and costs' to emphasize inclusion of all significant consequences; commenters debated the label but OMB emphasizes transparent listing of categories regardless of term.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of non-monetized (unquantified) benefits, costs, and transfers
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies should identify and discuss important non-quantified effects whenever presenting quantified costs or benefits, including a summary table of unquantified/non-monetized items.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include a summary table listing all unquantified or non-monetized benefits, costs, and transfers, and when feasible highlight those believed most important (e.g., by certainty, expected magnitude, reversibility). The table should not substitute for a narrative discussion of the most important non-quantified effects. Agencies should clearly communicate when monetized net-benefit figures do not reflect all important benefits or costs (OMB encourages clear communication but does not require a formal 'warning label').

rubrics_metrics.name: Monetizing health and safety benefits and costs (VSL, VSLY, child valuation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Material on monetizing health and safety (nonfatal risks, fatality risks, risks to children) remained largely unchanged; OMB recognizes ongoing academic debate and evolving methods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Given unsettled empirical and methodological issues (VSL, VSLY, valuing child mortality), OMB defers prescriptive changes and will work with agencies in specific analyses; it removed conflicting/redundant material and kept reliance on longstanding agency practice while inviting updates from agencies and the literature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of statistical life (VSL) and income dependence
rubrics_metrics.description: OMB recommended that it is appropriate to use a VSL that does not depend on the income of the sub-population receiving mortality risk reductions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OMB found arguments for mortality-risk-equity persuasive given conceptual difficulties with adjusting VSL by subgroup income and consistency with prior agency practice; commenters criticized and supported this approach—agencies should be aware of debate and rationale when applying VSL.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of general equilibrium modeling
rubrics_metrics.description: The revised Circular included new material about the potential role of general equilibrium modeling in benefit-cost analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies may consider general equilibrium approaches where appropriate; the Circular provides high-level discussion but leaves detailed methodological choices to agencies based on context and data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Projection of non-market environmental goods over time
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies should project values of non-market environmental goods accounting for the income elasticity of WTP and limited substitutability between non-market and market goods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Due to the heterogeneity of non-market goods, OMB declined to provide a default rate for how values change over time; agencies should apply context-specific projections reflecting income elasticity and substitutability assumptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accounting for compliance and take-up (compliance modeling)
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulatory analyses should consider likely compliance behavior (under-compliance, over-compliance, full compliance), anticipatory compliance, and take-up dynamics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider continuous monitoring approaches, disaggregate impacts driven by anticipatory compliance, and model incomplete compliance when strong evidence supports it. Examine risks of non-compliance, methods to promote compliance (including alternative rule designs), and the resources needed for compliance communications and enforcement. Consider distributional effects of uneven compliance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disaggregate anticipatory compliance effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies should disaggregate impacts driven by anticipatory compliance from other impacts of the regulation when relevant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Separating anticipatory effects can clarify the mechanisms by which regulation affects outcomes and improve realism of estimates; include such disaggregation when supported by evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of business cycle dynamics in benefit-cost estimation
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies should account for business cycle dynamics when estimating a regulation’s benefits and costs where relevant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expanded draft material on this topic was supported by commenters; agencies should include macroeconomic/business-cycle considerations in models and sensitivity analyses as appropriate to the regulatory context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Approach to transfers in summary accounting
rubrics_metrics.description: Two acceptable approaches: (1) present transfers as a separate category distinct from benefits and costs, or (2) treat transfers as offsetting benefits and costs (leaving net benefits unchanged).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OMB retained both approaches to provide flexibility so agencies can choose the approach that best fits the context; treating transfers as offsets may be especially useful for distributional analyses because welfare impacts depend on the distribution of transfers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guidance/question for classifying transfers ('naturally dollar-denominated' test)
rubrics_metrics.description: The draft suggested asking whether effects are 'naturally dollar-denominated' as a heuristic for identifying transfers (e.g., if not dollar-denominated, unlikely to be transfers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This heuristic provoked criticism (e.g., tangible goods with dollar transactions), and commenters recommended revising or deleting it; agencies should exercise care when using such heuristics and consider a range of factors in classifying transfers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of transfers (financial-exchange-only view contested)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some commenters argued transfers should be limited to financial receipts and payments; others warned that transferring could be used to downplay impacts on certain groups.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OMB retained flexibility and did not adopt a strict financial-exchange-only definition; agencies should be transparent about classification choices and consider behavioral consequences that may turn transfers into net benefits or costs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Behavioral responses to transfers
rubrics_metrics.description: Transfers often induce behavioral changes that generate benefits or costs beyond the transfer itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When transfers are expected to prompt behavioral responses, agencies should account for resulting benefits and costs rather than treating transfers as neutral accounting items.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use (and limitations) of the marginal cost of public funds (MCPF) in regulatory analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: OMB counsels against using the marginal cost of public funds (MCPF) in the primary regulatory analysis due to practical and theoretical challenges.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reasons include underspecification (distortionary cost depends on tax form), attribution indeterminacy (Congress, not agencies, decides future tax/spending choices), and omission of distributional considerations in many MCPF estimates. Agencies should generally not apply MCPF in primary net-benefit calculations, though they may discuss related issues qualitatively or in supplementary analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expanded guidance on producing distributional analyses
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies should produce distributional analyses when relevant to understand incidence and disparate effects across subpopulations; distributional analysis is critical to assessing full welfare effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Executive Orders direct consideration of distributive impacts and equity; OMB provides expanded guidance intended to assist agencies in estimating disparate effects. Agencies should consider which subpopulations are relevant, what metrics to use, and how distributional outcomes affect policymaking; OMB did not mandate universal requirements but encouraged broader use of distributional analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unit of analysis and granularity choices for distributional effects
rubrics_metrics.description: When choosing unit of analysis, agencies should consider whether the unit could obscure relevant distributional effects (e.g., using household vs individual units).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No one-size-fits-all rule: agencies may choose less granular units if data quality, reliability, comparability, or other concerns justify it, but should weigh tradeoffs and justify choices. Use the most granular data feasible in many cases, but balance against data quality and consistency across benefit and cost categories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of most granular information when feasible (but not mandatory)
rubrics_metrics.description: Commenters urged the use of the most granular information about benefits and costs feasible; OMB agreed that granularity is valuable but declined to issue blanket guidance requiring it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies should favor granular data where it improves accuracy and helps reveal distributional impacts, but may use less granular data for quality, comparability, or practicality reasons; document and justify granularity decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Whether to require distributional analyses
rubrics_metrics.description: Some commenters argued distributional analysis should be required as part of any complete BCA; OMB considered but did not adopt a universal requirement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OMB provided expanded guidance to facilitate distributional analysis and left agencies discretion to determine when and how to conduct detailed distributional work, recognizing practical constraints and varied agency missions.
